entry.title: Reversing Prediabetes
entry.content:
Background

I was thin all my childhood.

When I was in medical college (2011-2017) my hostel was near Kukkarhalli Kere in Mysuru and I used to run around the lake in the mornings. That loop was 3.8 km in my memory and I used to be able to finish it without stopping. I also used to cycle from hostel to college and back throughout the college days.

In internship and later in Vivekananda Memorial Hospital, I was always running around in patient care. Moreover, in VMH, there was a ground where I would occasionally go running too, especially preparing for a running race that was held to raise awareness on road accidents.

When I moved to Bengaluru in 2018, for the first couple of years, I was moving around a lot juggling my career in clinical medicine and software development, often visiting two offices on the same day, and usually taking public transport everywhere.

When COVID lockdown started in 2020, the sedentary part of my life started. By the end of 2022 with all the COVID lockdowns, I had developed myopia and started wearing glasses, and also developed a potbelly and a rounder face

I was clearly consuming more energy than I was spending. On March 12, 2024 my HbA1c was 5.9%. This put me in prediabetes. Something had to change.

Changing things

By April, I got a gear cycle from my brother. At that time I was often going to SOCHARA giving them a strategy and vision for digital humanities. It was 8km from my home.

On April 10, 2024 I started riding cycle on that commute.

By October that year, I had done this route about 22 times in each direction. This streak broke when I fell from scooter (should have stuck to cycle) once and started getting backache.

In 2025 I didn’t have this commute anymore and it was very difficult to convince myself to go to the park near my home for walk/jog. That’s when I developed the second part of my fitness regime and started doing jogs in the evenings (or whenever my mind allowed). I also did some rock climbing sessions. Lots of walking. Basically, I was active wherever possible.

I also started eating 1 chappatti less (from 3 to 2), only taking 1 serving of rice, and in general being only 70-80% full.

I got some gear too. A smart watch with GPS, running shoes, phone armband, running clothes.

Initially (let’s say August 2025) I could barely run 1km. I was running in wooden park in Indiranagar where a loop is just under 400m. So, I was running 2 rounds.

By a month, I was able to consistently run 2-3 rounds (in about 10 minutes).

By the end of 2025, I would try to run 4 continuous rounds (about a mile?) and it would take me around 20 minutes.

By Februrary 2026 I was able to increase to 6 rounds (2.5km) in about 30 minutes.

On 21 February, 2026 my HbA1c was 5.6% (not prediabetic anymore). But the journey is no longer about that.

By April 2026, I was able to run the same in about 20 minutes.

The first time I ran 7 continuous rounds in wood park was in May 2026 (24 minutes).

Then in July 2026, I did a 5k around Kukkarahalli Kere with daktre.

This gave me the confidence to run longer in wood park too, and I ran 10 rounds in 35 minutes. I repeated this yesterday (September 2026).

I feel a bit lighter around my belly, and also have no difficulty in climbing stairs, or having a long day of walking around nowadays.

Goals

Strava automatically tags other people running with us. In wood park sometimes I get strangers tagged with me. When I began running, I had once noticed someone like this, who had run 10 rounds (while I was running 4). At that time, it seemed like I would never be able to run 10 rounds. But here I am.

My pace now is about 41 minutes for 5K (if I extrapolate my 10 rounds), which is 8:20 per km.

Daktre routinely runs about 35 minutes for 5K. (7:00 km).

Yesterday I saw Thejesh’s goal of running 5K under 30 minutes, which is 6:00 per km.

The present world record for 5K is 12:35.36 which is 2:31 per km.

When Sabastian Sawe broke marathon (42.195 km) world record in 2026 London Marathon, he ran 5K in 14:14 (which is 2:51 per km).

I’m definitely not breaking any world records soon. But I will keep progressing till I plateau.

I’m also starting to progress in pull-ups and weights. Let’s see where we go from here.

entry.title: Moon Monday #292: An obsessively linked rundown of recent global lunar exploration and cooperation updates
entry.content:
Mission updates

  • The launch of China’s Chang’e 7 mission, intending to systematically study water ice on the Moon, was first delayed from late August 2026 to September due to poor weather conditions from a tropical depression but later delayed entirely to early next year without CMSA stating any specific reason. Jack Congram notes that the delay does take place against the background of quality issues facing China’s launch vehicles this year, amid otherwise successful streaks. The Sino government says it’s keen on resolving issues across the board.
  • This means the next lunar mission launching this year could thus be Astrobotic’s large Griffin CLPS lander, which aims to land on the Moon’s south pole. It will deploy the FLIP rover by Astrolab (a Moon Monday sponsor), who onboarded last year after NASA decided not to fly the critical VIPER rover for studying water ice aboard Griffin. FLIP is yet to be integrated with Griffin, which will take place pre-launch at SpaceX’s facilities. Astrobotic has so far shared that it has integrated three of the other lander payloads: NASA’s Navigation Doppler LiDAR (NDL) which will aid Griffin’s navigation, the company’s own CubeRover, and ESA’s LandCam-X which will help improve landing precision. Astrobotic was acquired by Voyager Technologies with a desire to position Griffin’s hoped-for success to bag more Artemis Moonbase contracts from NASA.
  • Eric Berger reports on an independent review of the performance of the Artemis II Orion capsule’s heat shield during its April descent to Earth with astronauts. The review found that NASA’s decision to change the reentry profile for reducing the shield’s material loss worked quite well since said loss was about an order of magnitude lower than seen during Artemis I.
Related: How NASA planned to keep Artemis II astronauts safe throughout their Moon mission 👨🏽‍🚀
  • China demonstrated optical laser communications between a lunar orbiter and Earth, as part of its efforts to build a lunar navigation and communications network. Here’s a comprehensive review of each major component China has demonstrated towards having such capabilities. China also announced a constellation of up to ~30 small satellites to monitor objects in cislunar (Earth-Moon) space and study the lunar environment, with foreign partners being invited to co-build satellites or payloads.
Related: A comprehensive review of each major component China has demonstrated towards having such capabilities. 🛰️
  • US-based Zeno Power Systems will fly a 5-watt Radioisotope Heater Unit (RHU) on a Firefly lunar lander, possibly on a 2028 mission to the Moon’s nearside as part of the NASA’s CLPS program.
  • The Advanced-Space-led and NASA-funded team behind the CAPSTONE-02 mission announced the successful completion of the Critical Design Review (CDR) phase. The mission aims to launch in 2027 and demonstrate rendezvous and docking of two satellites in lunar orbit as well as advance autonomous navigation capabilities.
  • Russia’s near-future lunar exploration plans still involve launching the polar reconnaissance orbiter of Luna 26. Its primary goal after launching circa 2027 is to map our Moon’s surface in multiple wavelengths at high resolutions. Luna 26 is expected to operate for one year in a low lunar orbit at 60 to 80 kilometers, and for two years in higher orbits of 150 to 200 kilometers. Luna 26 will particularly help scientists better grasp the distribution of water ice on the Moon’s poles, which will be useful data to help plan the China-led ILRS Moonbase project of which Russia is a member. Another major goal of Luna 26 is to measure and characterize the radiation and plasma environment around the Moon. Luna 26’s instruments are listed below.
  • Jack Congram reports that launch complex infrastructure at the Wenchang spaceport for China’s Long March 10 rocket, which will launch taikonauts to the Moon, has been progressing well ahead of a first robotic test launch in H2 2027.

Cooperation and collaboration

  • A joint German-US-Israeli study has found that on NASA’s Artemis I mission, the test vest worn by a mannequin onboard the Orion spacecraft was effective at reducing radiation exposure by ~50%. The result is promising for using similar protective vests on long-duration lunar and deep space missions in the future, especially when solar storms pass through the Earth-Moon space. This study complements another Artemis I radiation evaluation, which found that radiation exposure to future astronauts will vary not only based on time spent at locations within the capsule but also on Orion’s orientation in space. For example, the paper said that when Orion’s orientation was altered during an engine burn, exposure levels dropped nearly in half due to the highly directional nature of the radiation in the Van Allen belt.
Related: How ISRO’s Chandrayaan 2 orbiter is a Sun watcher at the Moon 🌗
  • The US-led Artemis Accords for cooperative lunar exploration and data sharing onboarded three more signatories—Serbia, Mauritius, and Turkey—while the US President claimed the Moon to be American territory. The latter went completely unreported by many western space and technology media outlets who otherwise cover equivalent statements by officials on the other side of the world. Anyway, the total number of signee nations of the Accords are now 71. The cancellation of the NASA-led Gateway international lunar habitat though has already previously demonstrated that the Accords have little bearing on preserving international partnerships in the Artemis program, much less flourishing them. ESA and Northrop Grumman are looking into repurposing their respective Gateway elements as independent lunar missions.
  • NASA invited India to join the Artemis Moonbase program. As has China last year for the ILRS Moonbase. So far, India has signed the Artemis Accords but not China’s equivalent program. ISRO has been aiding NASA in crewed Moon landing site selections for Artemis. Any new cooperation intent though is only on paper for now so we will have to wait and see what actually manifests as time goes by.
Related: How the Chandrayaan 2 orbiter helped Japan nail SLIM’s Moon landing 🎯
  • In collaboration with IBM and several academic institutions, NASA has launched open-source AI models built specifically to aid lunar science. Trained primarily on sections of data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), the agency claims that the open models will help accelerate geologic studies of the Moon.
  • China has established joint laboratories with Thailand and Serbia for lunar science and exploration studies.
  • An overview of international mechanisms related to the Moon

Many thanks to Catalyx Space and Elisa Perednia of ILOA for sponsoring Moon Monday. If you too appreciate my efforts to bring you this curated community resource on global lunar exploration for free, and without ads, kindly support my independent writing as it’s purely reader-funded. I don’t use AI to write a single word and cite everything.

entry.title: Healing Earth Workshop 2026 at Ashoka
entry.content:
I recently got to attend the Healing Earth Workshop 2026 along with my colleagues Smayan and Naveen from FPLaunchpad.

As someone coming primarily from a computer science background, this was useful in understanding the domain knowledge that we need as part of the ESG (environment, social, and governance) applications research group in our lab.

Day 1

Day 1 was the workshop on the science of climate change.

Tiny Shells, Deep Time: How Marine Carbonates Record Earth’s Climate - by Prof. Sambuddha Mishra

The first talk was on Foraminifera (or forams) by Prof. Sambuddha Mishra. Forams are marine oragnisms with a Calcium Carbonate shell. These shells get deposited as sediment. Since evolving more than half a billion years ago, their shells -- and the corresponding sediments -- have also evolved due to the changing climate over these millions of years. In marine regions where the sediment has not been greatly disturbed (e.g. by an incoming river), a core sample can be studied to identify the historical climate conditions with our knowledge of the chemistry of Foraminifera shells of the time. This analysis tells us with some error range what the temperatures must have been like.

I learnt that temperatures were a lot hotter (by up to 16 degrees Celsius) about 50 million years ago, and we have since had colder and hotter periods. However, the rate at which the Earth has been warming since the industrial revolution is unprecedented. The slope of the temperature change from 10,000 years ago until 1850s is comparable to the slope of the temperature change since the industrial revolution until now (but increasing vs. decreasing).

How Mangroves Lock Away Carbon—and Why It Matters - by Prof. Indra Shekar Sen

Prof. Indra Shekar Sen spoke about the role mangroves play in storing carbon, the kinds of mangrove forests that exist, and the work needed to restore them.

Some important points he made:

  • Since the industrial revolution, the burning of fossil fuels specifically has been the largest contributor for CO$_2$ increase and rising temperatures.
  • Soils hold thrice as much carbon as the atmosphere
  • Permafrost -- frozen soil -- are special in that they hold ~50% of organic soil despite only covering ~15% of soil land. This is important because this organic matter has not been decomposed further only due to cold temperatures. If this warms -- and poles warm faster than the equator -- then microbes will get to act on this matter and release more CO$_2$ as a byproduct of the decomposition, thereby contributing to global warming.
  • Anoxia is a total oxygen depletion.
  • In mangroves, under a very thin oxygenated surface, there is anoxia in the sediment. This means that carbon stored there will not get converted into CO$_2$ by usual decomposition pathways.
  • The carbon composition of mangroves is approximately:
    • Above-ground: 10%
    • Below-ground: 5%
    • Soil sediment: 85%
  • From a restoration angle, mangrove forests can be classified as degraded, restored, and old-mature.
  • Old & mature mangroves are very good at locking carbon (through anoxia, as mentioned above)
  • Degraded mangroves can be restored with human efforts but will take much effort and time (decades) to become as good as old & mature mangroves at carbon preservation

From intuition to technological solutions to environmental problems - by Prof. Meghna Agarwala

Prof. Meghna Agarwala spoke about examples of technological interventions to convey that we should understand the local context and nuances before intervening.

Her first case study was of pine trees in Himachal and Nepal. Historical records indicate that pine was not native to the altitudes they studied (300m-3,000m). These plantations were done around 1970s and after as part of the national policy on climate change intervention. This however has had bad consequences for the local ecosystems because:

  • grazing lands were converted to pine-forest lands, impacting existing local livelihoods
  • pine trees are more susceptible to fires
  • natural regeneration was better in some areas and reached 99-100% cover

She further adds that increasing canopy height or canopy cover would not be useful in most areas in India because most of our forests are savannas / open natural ecosystems. We should not purely chase plantation cover but look at the local ecology and livelihoods.

Another consequence she adds is the human-wildlife conflict introduced when nuance is not understood. She gave the examples of elephants -- who prefer low-canopy forests. In Odisha, there are roughly 200 human deaths and 50 elephant deaths in a year.

Carbon, Commodity, Community: the Science and Practice of Nature-based Solutions - by Prof. Ghazala Shahabuddin

Prof. Ghazala speaks about nature-based solutions (NBS). A central point was that higher biodiversity -- the species richness -- tends to have higher carbon sequestration as well. She criticised the transactional, itemised carbon trading systems that ignore the local biodiversity and ecology.

She gave an example of a study that estimated the _metric tons of CO$2$ that can be removed by eliminating Lianas -- long-stemmed vines -- from trees in a forest. This is disturbing because it takes away from the local diversity.

Another example she gave was of Gujarat where Google purchased carbon credits to remove 100,000 tonnes from a firm called Varaha. The vendor's pathway for that was to remove trees of an invasive species (Prosopis juliflora), convert them into biochar, and bury that biochar under the soil. The hypothesis is that under the soil, this biochar will store carbon for centuries. One unintended consequence of this has been that because biochar retains soil moisture, this benefits the same invasive Prosopis tree over native grass.

I found this article that speaks of the same issue.

I liked her warning about measuring climate change and mitigation through a single and incomplete metric such as carbon score, but to understand the long-term benefits and harms of our actions. Ecosystems are more complex than a single metric can capture; and destroying ecology in one region cannot often be compensated by actions in other regions, especially without understanding the regional ecologies.

Climate change & infectious disease modelling - by Prof. Gautam Menon

Prof. Gautam spoke about climate change as a public health risk directly because the survival and transmission of many pathogens is also dependent on the climatic conditions.

For example, malaria has a certain temperature range under which it survives, and a temperature at which it is optimal. The relationship between transmission and temperature for malaria is modelled by the Briere equation. This graph has a gradual build-up till optimal and then a steep fall.

He also spoke about STH - soil-transmitted helminths - as neglected tropical diseases. About 1 billion people are susceptible to this.

More participation, less AI: Lessons from the CoRE stack - by Prof. Aaditeshwar Seth

We at FPL are collaborating with Prof. Aaditeshwar Seth's initiative for applying computer science knowledge to social problems. He was super kind to us, and generous with his time during the breaks where we got to introduce each other and discuss about the projects we could work on.

In this talk, he spoke about their bottom-up methodology they use in CoRE-stack. I have also been thinking about PDGI and PDI, and CoRE-stack's work is an important case study. Some important points from his talk:

  • community-based problem discovery:
    • this is important to do - but I also imagine difficult to operationalize. I think their landscape stewards and interactions with local communities play a major part in this.
  • active in >2,000 villages
  • disconnect in individual good vs collective good
  • disconnect between top-down vs bottom-up decision making
    • for example with government initiatives, planning is done at the top and implementation is expected to be identical everywhere
    • this misses local complexities
  • a better model is when there can be guidance from the top, and local communities can be empowered to plan on their own
  • communities should to be empowered to make decisions at their level
    • there may be power-based inequalities such as with local elite groups that capture resources and schemes
  • we should build a model where local knowledge and domain-expertise can be used to make better decisions
  • the Commons Connect app can be used to explore geospatial datasets and relevant geotagged data
    • then add local knowledge
    • produce DPRs - Detailed Project Reports
    • then this DPR can be submitted at Gram Sabha, and then Gram Panchayat

entry.title: Weeknote September 07 - September 14 2026
entry.content:
Depression got hands

Last week was not the best and most of it was spent tending to my own mental health.

When Monday rolled around something was off and I could not pinpoint what had happened but I spent most of my time trying to recover from that mindset.

I spiralled a bit here and there, but what really helped was journalling. My handwriting is chicken scratch and when I am particularly in the hole so to speak, it becomes closer to the scratchings you would find in the dirary of some cultist worshipping an Eldritch abomination.

So what do I do while dealing with depression? I mostly rest, I know that it goes counter to a lot of advice which people recieve, but I know my body and I know that If I don't take a break, my body will force me to take one. My mind feels heavy is how I would describe it where ambiguous inputs are interpreted negatively. So I usually will be losing HP every time I have an interaction and I can't figure out if it is going good or bad.

So while I live a pretty reginmented life, I sometimes take a day off and just close my eyes and lie on the floor. It feels nice and grounding because there is no interaction.

That doesn't mean that I don't work out, quite the opposite in fact.

I am technically the lowest weight I have been in a long time. Obviously there is a long way to go but I am not going to binge eat myself to feel better!

I also want to share that I can deadlift a 100KGs which isn't much to brag about, but it is the first time in my life that I have lifted something in triple digits. So the funny thing is that I feel physically the best I have ever felt but mentally I was not doing good.

I really wanted to get back into gamedev, but I could tell that whatever I was feeling didn't really want to me to do anything creative. I don't know why this happens.

So the times where I wasn't on the floor I spent studying for interviews and applying for jobs.

The two highlights of my week happened on Sunday.

Firstly I met my friends for Badminton, and since it's been a long time since we played it felt good. Socializing is good, self isolation is bad, who would have thought??

Secondly I went to see an indie documentary about independant candidates in politics. The director and documentarian are people I have been following for quite some time. The idea of people fighting for their rights in the fringes of the country and succeeding or failing and how politics works in these regions was illuminating. Since it's part 1 of 4 I can only imagine how much better the director and documentarian will be getting. I am wishing them the best because they are genuine in what they want for the country.

entry.title: Things You Might Not Know About This Website
entry.content:
Over the years, this website has accumulated many interesting and atypical features and pages. Most visitors either browse the homepage or land on individual posts from syndications and social media, and never click around enough to notice and experience all the intriguing things scattered around the website. So I decided to jot some of them down in this note1.

This post was originally published on abhinavsarkar.net.

Similar/Different Posts
Each post links to other posts that are most similar, as well as, most different to it, as a way to let the visitors explore the website. For example, see the similar and different posts for this very post. You may also notice the green bars behind the post dates that show the measure of similarity2.

Post Comment Feeds
Visitors can comment on the posts using the built-in comment form. Each post has a dedicated feed of its comments to which the visitors can subscribe, for example, this very post’s comment feed.

Calendar Archive
The Archive page shows all posts and notes on this website as a year-by-month calendar. Clicking on the links shows the post details. This page lets the visitor see the entire history of my writing in one glance.

Head Radio
A log of songs that spontaneously start playing in my head. Comes with a feed for you to follow.

Site Graph
An interactive graph of major pages in the website that shows how the pages are connected to each-other. You can click any node in the graph to navigate to its page. The graph can also be filtered by content types.

Outgoing Links
A list of all external links from my posts to the internet websites, auto-extracted and with its own feed.

Linkblog Search
My Linkblog supports searching the full text of the linked posts. Yup, the posts that are not on my website. I frequently use it myself.

Drafts and Ideas
The Upcoming page lists all my draft posts and post ideas, and visitors can vote on them anonymously to let me know what they want me to work on.

Feeds List
This website has Atom feeds for almost every content list in it. The Feeds page lists all feeds in the websites, with 17 main feeds, and scores of tagwise feeds3.

Activities Page
The Activities page lists the recent physical activities I have done, and also shows yearly bar charts for each activity type. The data is pulled from Strava.

Self-hosted Slides
Slides of some talks I’ve presented are hosted right here on this website. I use remark.js to create them. They are also embedded in their corresponding talks pages and can be viewed inline. An example talk: Functional Programming Patterns and its slides.

Dead-link Archiving
All external links in the posts and the Linkblog are automatically checked every day, and the dead ones are rewritten to point to the Wayback Machine snapshots.

Many more small features and tidbits are sprinkled throughout the website. The Colophon page lists some, but not all, of them. Honestly, I love having my own website and adding these small embellishments around. This is the magic of IndieWeb!

If you have any questions or comments, please leave a comment below. If you liked this post, please share it. Thanks for reading!

  1. This post is inspired by Shellsharks’ post Things You Might Not Know About This Site about their own website.↩︎

  2. The similarity between posts is calculated using Cosine similarity between TF-IDF vectors of the text of all posts. This is done at the website build time by my static site generator.↩︎

  3. The EVERYTHING feed is a combined feed of all feeds on this website, providing a firehose of all activities in one place. I don’t recommend subscribing to it.↩︎

Thanks for reading this post via feed. Feeds are great, and you're great for using them. ♥

entry.title: Improve the RSS experience of your blog readers
entry.content:
I love RSS feeds. And if you do too, here are some things you should considering offering to readers of your blog, newsletter, or website to advance the Independent Web:

  1. Introduce people to RSS readers in an accessible way and link to such an explainer on your /feeds page and /subscribe page. In both cases, don’t assume people know or understand the term. When introducing people you know to RSS readers, don’t assume how or what they read and consume on the Web. The concept of an agnostic feed reader can be hard to understand or appreciate for people at first so make sure you understand the person’s habits and needs before suggesting anything. Only then do you see that glimmer in their eyes when lightning strikes. When I listen to people’s reading workflows first, and only then suggest a feed reader and how & where it could benefit them, do I hear the tech click.
  2. Subscribing to RSS feeds remains an inconsistent experience even if you know about this amazing technology. Offer direct subscription links for various popular feed readers on your blog’s /feeds page.
  3. Include the link to such a page in your blog’s persistent header or footer menu for discoverability. If you have social media icons or links, an RSS page link should be there too. Also include said link in your newsletter’s form and footer so people always have a subscription choice. Doing this is good for you too for when someone wants to unsubscribe from your post emails specifically but keep following otherwise.
  4. Provide full-content RSS feeds instead of posts showing just a title and excerpt. This is also useful for accessibility setups.
  5. Add a footer menu in your blog’s RSS feeds so that people can visit your About page, contact you, or explore your blog after they’re done reading a post. Don’t make them jump through unintuitive clicks for the basics. The reading and interacting experience should be as if people have come to visit your blog directly. I’ve thus added footer menus in the RSS feeds of both my space blog and personal blog, possible thanks to kind technical help from Abhinav Sarkar at an IndieWebClub BLR session.

This microblog you’re reading, which is on Pagecord, sadly doesn’t have a footer menu in its RSS feed or newsletter because the platform doesn’t offer a way to customize them.

  1. If you post on your blog about multiple things, or if you post frequently, everyone would not be interested in everything you share. Offer an RSS feed of the most important or the most publicly relevant post type you publish so readers can choose the slice of your thoughts they like best. As such, I offer a feed specifically for Moon Monday since that’s my flagship writing.
  2. If you move blogging platforms, always ensure you redirect the old feed URL to the new one, including URL variations as well as links of category feeds and such.
  3. Thank your readers for using the best, most ethical reading technology on the Internet. 🤓

entry.title: Weeknotes: Week #37 (2026)
entry.content:
This week was a bit all over the place with work being a little weird, and me spending most of my free time working on Claw. Lots of cooking though!

Personal

Not a lot of socializing this week, since I mostly worked from home and opted to be a homebody. In total, I spent around 2 hours talking to my parents over voice and video calls which is a big change for me. It was rather pleasant! Though I will admit, learning that they’re planning a trip to Bhubaneswar via orders to book their flights was a little annoying.

On Thursday night we picked up a package from one friend for another and chatted a bit, was nice to catch up.

I needed to buy a new pair of shoes so Yash and I did that together on Sunday afternoon to get some time under the sun. 1 PM was a little hot for this but the walk was enjoyable. The Skechers store here in Indirangar didn’t have the best collection, but I was able to find something acceptable.

Work

Things at work have been rather quiet as everyone is in the middle of long duration projects and the day-to-day has slowed down quite a lot. The next Monday being a holiday will be nice, given I have 3 straight hours of meetings on Tuesday, starting at 8:30 AM. I suppose this is my pre-training for an eventual managerial position, which is not serving its intended purpose as far as I am concerned.

Movies

With most lunchtimes being at home, the second monitor had some movies going. I watched Crime 101 which was decent enough but rather formulaic. Top Gun: Maverick was up next and once again it’s just Tom Cruise being excellently Tom Cruise. On the homelab side, my KVM which I use for my home server kept losing the HDMI signal randomly, and I finally decided to fix this issue once and for all.

Turns out even after changing the iGPU settings in BIOS, they were not being respected for some reason and hence I wasn’t getting any signal. I manually forced the iGPU to be enabled by putting the kernel parameter in /boot/syslinux/syslinux.cfg:

video=HDMI-A-1:1920x1080@60e

The important part is the e at the end, which stands for enabled. The KVM got a signal once I rebooted :)

Life

Paryushan

My main reason for visiting home is attending the Paryushan Mahaparv, maha means big and parv means festival. Basically, Paryushan is the name and we call it "big festival" :). It's a 8 day festival celebrated by the followers of Jainism, where we increase our usual spiritual activities along side fasting, bhakti (singing devotion songs to the God), pakshal, puja etc. One important distinction between usual Hindu fasting and ours is we do not eat any food, NONE, no fruits, no milk, no sabudana, nothing. It's a fast with water only diet. Water itself has rules too. It needs to boiled water (consumption after cooling down ofc :P), and can only be drank between 48 minutes after sunrise to 48 minutes before sunset! These are the rules we strictly follow when doing Tapasya(jain fasting).

Everyday people daunt at the idea of staying hungry for 16-18 hours, while Jains have young kids not eating anything for a month! Its called Maskhaman in our language! There are fasting periods longer than this too, but that's where most of the people stop. There's a special name for a fasting period of 8 days called Atthai. Loads of people do Atthai during Paryushan. And the next step down is Telu/Attham. This is where you fast for three days. And finally you are down to 2 and 1 days called Chhat and Upvasa respectively.

I had done an Atthai when I got my first job, I still remember asking my manager to delay my joining by a week because I knew I would feel so weak that my brain would stop working. Btw, before this long fast, I had only ever done Upvasas (one-day fasts) in my life. Hence, I consider myself a bit lucky that I survived Atthai without anything bad happening 😅. This time I did a Telu i.e. three days, in fact I just did a Parna (meal that ends the fast) before writing this weeknote xD.

I would definitely write about my experience, but to create some hype around the same and answer reader's wonder a bit, I did not get hunger pangs AT ALL! Jains have mastered the art of fasting and it is definitely worth a try listening to their words on the same :).

entry.title: Why Garmin Forerunner 965?
entry.content:
I have been looking for a full-fledged smartwatch for a while now. I have a Pebble and a BangleJS; I use them all the time. But they are semi-smartwatches. I wanted a full-fledged watch that lasts for days and works fully offline. This post isn’t a review; that will take time. This one is more like why I chose the 965. Before I go any further, let me list out my requirements.

Requirements

  • Known and proven brands that have supported the hardware for at least a decade. And not known for dropping products. No Google, Apple, or Samsung.
  • It’s meant for outdoor use, so at least semi-rugged. Buttons and not just touch screen. Good readable screen.
  • Good battery life
  • It should work without a phone for at least a few days. I.e., good offline functionality. It should work without a network for sure.
  • GPS and Offline Maps. Ability to run GPS/Maps for at least 24 hours.
  • Good community, openness
  • Cost. I had a fairly high budget of 50K.

Solution

I looked into Garmin, Coros, and Casio.

I chose the Garmin Forerunner 965. Other watches I considered were the Garmin Instinct 3, the Garmin Fenix® 7X Pro, and the Coros Nomad. I considered the Casio ProTek (WSD-F20) series, but neither the community nor the OS seemed interesting enough. But I do love how rugged they are. I will keep an eye on them.

Garmin Instinct 3 has everything except offline maps. It has a cool screen and GPS. But it has no routeable maps. It’s also expensive. Garmin Fenix® 7X Pro is better in every way, but it’s double the cost and weight. Coros Nomad is the closest competitor; it has all the features I wanted, at a similar price, and it’s rugged and pretty. But I don’t know anything about Coros; no one I know has it. Also, I don’t know much about the community around it. It’s also the brand that is on my list.

I was able to load Indian OSM maps onto my Forerunner 965. I have used it while running and for casual walking. I haven’t done much routing on the watch, though it’s possible. I could follow a GPX track easily. I will blog more. Overall, these features seem to work.

Everything on the phone works offline and also works without the phone. Of course, you can send messages without the phone (it doesn’t have a network), but it can connect to Wi-Fi if needed. It can also store music and play it through my Bluetooth earbuds. So you can go out without the phone.

I have not charged the watch much. I am quite active every day, so it’s not bad. I haven’t taken it out for a full day of motorcycling or trekking with maps/routing on. When I do that, I will write more.

The community around it is good, though they are more focused on outdoor activities and mapping. I haven’t explored their apps yet.

As I said, this is not a review. This is just the list of things that I looked for while buying this watch, held up against them. For how it performs in those areas, you will have to wait. And it won’t be a single blog post. For now, there are no red flags with the Forerunner 965.

entry.title: Taking care of my devices, and myself
entry.content:
I own three major devices: A MacBook, an iPhone, and a Kindle. The MacBook Air has served me well for almost six years now. The iPhone 15 for two and a half years. The Kindle Paperwhite for three and a half years. I want all of these devices to last as long as they can. With that in mind, I decided to get good covers and/or cases to better protect them all. The other desire is to improve my body posture when using or holding these devices. As such, it's good if they can have better self-support.

  • For the Kindle, I got a magnetic Transformer case from ProElite. Its origami-style folding to make the Kindle stand in portrait and landscape is outstanding. The case has improved my long duration reading sessions multi-fold. All puns intended.
  • For the MacBook, I got a two-part case which protects all the edges of the top and bottom sections. It also provides rubber feet for the base, which is great because my MacBook's feet have worn out over the years.
  • For the iPhone, I got a rubberized case with corner protection and a metal-ring stand so it can hold itself on any flat surface. I got this from the local market.

The fact that these cases made the devices bulkier is a plus point. I now prefer using the Kindle and the phone with their stands on, which has drastically improved my posture for the majority of my usage. The laptop case making my MacBook slightly bulkier, and its rubber feet being sturdy again now, means I use it on my lap even less than I used to.

Jailbreaking my Kindle means I can do a few more things on it now thanks to KOReader and its community, such as writing poetry or short notes which I would've otherwise had to use my laptop or phone for. I now write on my Kindle with a nice bluetooth keyboard at home, and when commuting, with a lightweight one that folds. This is a win for my eyes through the epaper display of the Kindle, and for my back because of not having to carry my laptop in some commutes.

P.S. The Amazon links are not affiliate links. They’re just so that people can see the product.

Even before I started using my Kindle to do some strain-free writing for my eyes, I've been having the display settings on my phone and laptop such that they are not screaming addictive colors in my face. I’ve enabled color filters to make the screen look pastel and pleasant, and paired it with high contrast and warm Night Light turned on. Of course, dark mode is always on too. But still, no matter how you tame it, you cannot change the fundamental nature of the beast that are LCD and LED screens. And you cannot beat the inborn zen of epaper displays. Looking at epaper still feels way more peaceful.

The Kindle's battery life is phenomenal, thanks in major part to the epaper display. Even with all the functionality I added post-jailbreak, and my increased usage, the battery still lasts for a week at least. This means my long writing sessions almost never need to worry about the charge level of the device. In fact, using the Kindle more also means I'm using the laptop and phone that much less, thereby extending the battery life I get out of both.

Don't get me wrong, it's not all rosy. The jailbroken Kindle and its epaper display are not perfect by any means. The slow refresh rate innate to the display can be frustrating several times a day. So can the extremely limited capabilities of the Kindle, even with KOReader enhancements, for getting basic tasks done compared to even a mobile OS. But the calm mental state epaper provides in return for patience is more valuable. It cares for your eyes. It makes you pay greater attention to the words of people when reading because there is nothing much in the device to distract you. And its limitations also force you to slow down, which is great for writing.

It's funny how the device that costs about five times less than my laptop or phone is the one that's most pleasurable to use. Constraints are great. Embrace them.

entry.title: Fantastic Dosas And Where To Find Them (in Bangalore) 2026 Edition
entry.content:
With over 27 years of experience in consuming and critiquing dosas from across South India, I consider it my personal responsibility to review and rank Bangalore's dosas each year, so that young, impressionable palates are able to differentiate hype from mastery.

Before we rank them, let me share three things. First, I am a Kannadiga from Mangalore (and Udupi) by blood but I was raised in Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu. Which means, unlike most of you, I love both sambars: the tangy, tamarind-forward, spicy, sharp Tamil sambar, and also the sweet, coconut-rich, jaggery-laced, Karnataka-style sambar. And I love both dosas, the thick, buttery, gently tangy Udupi-style dosas I grew up around, and the thin, crispy, rice-forward Tamil dosa. They are my two eyes, I have seen the world through both of them, and will never be able to choose one over the other. Second, the experience of eating the dosa matters to me as much as the taste and quality of the dosa, which means I don’t want to feel like I’m rushing through my meal desperately in a refugee camp. Third, please remember that there is no “correct” kind of dosa. Every culture down south has their own kind and there’s plenty of variety. With that disclaimer, let us get to ranking the best dosas in Bangalore in 2026.

At number six comes the Ghee Dosa at Shree Krishna Kafe in Koramangala. This was the first outstanding Tamil dosa I ate in Bangalore, and it continues to endure, holding its own against hordes of ghee-flooded dosas. A cute girl once used this to dosa to seduce me and it worked. She is gone but this dosa is often on my mind. So why does Shree Krishna rank so highly? SKK offers crisp dosas made from the quintessential Tamil dosa batter. Their sambar is heavy with dhal and flavour and spices, while their coconut chutney has almost none, allowing the latter to stay in the background as a vital supporting actor. They use quality ingredients, avoid dumping soda into their food, and let you leave the restaurant feeling full and healthy, as opposed to the debaucherous feeling that one feels after eating at Rameshwaram Cafe. SKK also makes the list because they offer seating and table service, so that you don’t feel stressed and rushed like refugee who is scrambling and fighting for a meal. I’ve always been happy that the dosa-hype-mob hasn’t found SKK and that food influencers are turned off by its humble interiors and terrible, anti-instagram lighting. The result is a relaxing dining experience. If you visit, make sure to also try their podi idli. Its special because the idli is tossed over and over in wok with ghee and curry leaves and spices, and the layer of red spice is charmed onto the idlis rather than coated onto it.

At number five comes the Pesarattu dosa at Babai Tiffins, HSR Layout. You didn't see that coming, did you? Pesarattu breaks from the Tamil and Karnataka styles: at Babai, it is a green-gram-and-rice dosa with a savoury, dense bite rather than the airy crispness of a classic fermented dosa. The peanut chutney is the right accompaniment: nutty, punchy and assertive enough to cut through the dosa’s richness. When I dream of this Pesarattu dosa, i see visions of its insides shining with with tiny bits of roasted onions.

At number four comes the Pudina Masala dosa at Sri Srinivasa Hotel in Basuvangudi. Yes they’re going to make you buy a token, wait for forty minutes, but its worth the wait. Its one of the genuinely unique dosas of our times. And its one the few dosa joints with long lines that does not spray 100ml of ghee onto your dosa to make it tasty. So what makes it so unique in my opinion? It is a crisp, butter-roasted dosa with a mint-forward potato filling: vivid green, aromatic and unlike the standard masala dosa. What stays in mind is the contrast: a heavy-handed butter roast delivers a shatteringly crisp exterior while the crumb underneath stays spongy (like really SPONGY) and thoroughly soaked in that herbaceous filling. Yes, not everyone likes palya, and that's why the palya-to-dosa ratio pulled tight enough that the mint never drowns out the crunch. You'll love and admire the contrast. And the spongy layer is so soft and wondrous that you'll think about it for the rest of your day. I must admit though that the wait times are horrendous and can dampen the experience. Go early, very early. And take a weird book with you and read it, and get asked about it, and make friends. You’ll build a reading habit, make a friend, and eat a wondrous dosa, that’s three birds with one dosa.

At number three comes the Davangere Benne Dosa at Sri Guru Kottureshwara Benne Dose in Vijaynagar. I want yout to forget all your impressions and experiences of the Davangere dosa from other restaurants, and I beg you to leave all your baggage behind as you begin the long journey to Vijaynagar to savor this dosa. Everything you’ve had before is a cheap copy, a counterfeit, a fraud, and a mockery. Cleanse your mind, wipe away all your old memories, and let your desire be reborn as you move towards this dosa. SGKBD has earned a serious reputation among Benne Dosa devotees for bringing a version of Davangere-style butter dosa to Bengaluru. The original outlet is opposite Bapuji Dental College in Davangere, and the Vijayanagar outlet was launched as the restaurant’s first Bengaluru branch. For the uninitiated, it is distinct from both the Tamil paper roast and the Mysore masala dosa: smaller, thicker and softer, closer to a buttery flatbread-dosa hybrid than a lacy crisp. It's paired with generous amounts of butter (not ghee) applied liberally to the tawa and the finished dosa, plus a side of mashed potato preparation, rather than the standard potato palya, and the signature coarse chutney. I cannot wait for you to taste these crispy, melt-in-your mouth dosas.

At number two comes the butter masala dosa at Airlines Hotel on Lavelle road. The fact that a restaurant sits under the canopy of a massive, 60-year old banyan tree alone should make it a treat to visit.It is a drive-in restaurant, with a lovely open-air garden and a history that reaches back to 1968. The Benne (Butter) Masala Dosa is the reason people still make the pilgrimage: a thin, crisp dosa laid with a generous, unapologetic slab of butter before the classic potato palya goes in, so the butter melts straight into the crumb rather than sitting decoratively on top. It is rich in the way only an old Bengaluru institution can get away with. And for those who like it spicy, the dosa features a light smear of kempu (red) chutney, so every bite gets a hit of it under the mellow potato. The filter coffee served here is excellent in both taste and presentation, and makes it to my Top 3 in Bangalore list. Airlines Hotel also has a divine connection for those interested. What do I mean by that? Given that you’re eating under a Banyan tree, there are dozens of birds above. And I’ve noticed that its a great way to test your karmic balance. Only the most rotten, selfish and cruel among you will be defecated upon mid-dosa. Those of you that are pure, righteous and have a heart that is not heavy with guilt, can eat freely without worry. Tis a great place for a first date, thanks to this acid test. Is that boy really that nice or does he operate from under a veil of deceit? The crows shall tell you.

At number one is the ghee dosa at The Filter Coffee, Indiranagar. Lets start with all the supporting elements that make this dosa one of the best. There’s ample seating, which means if you’re dining as a larger group, you’ll have a comfortable experience (though there is a wait time). The lighting and ambience and vibe are quite nice. And most importantly, there are seats by the kitchen counter that let you watch as your food is being prepared. You can hear the fiery sizzle of water hitting the dosa kal as it is being refreshed by the dosa master. You’ll see him spin and spread the batter like an artisan, spray it with ghee, scoop masala onto it, and garnish it with with chopped greens and onions, and even wait patiently as he watches the dosa cook into its final form. The ghee dosa and ghee masala here are exceptional. They come with some delectable accompaniments: authentic sambar, perfect milky-white coconut chutney, and some exciting green chutney (kothamalli) and orange chutney (small onion and chilli base). Their other hits include the Venn Pongal, and their phenomenal idlis which are solid in hand but melt once in your mouth. Their coffee is also good and serves as a nice finish to a hearty meal.

Legendary dosas that exist above and beyond this list:

The Masala Dosa at MTR is one of my all-time favourites. I eat it almost every other month, almost out of duty. It is unlike anything else on this list. The dosa is made with red rice and urad dal instead of the usual parboiled rice. A green chutney masala is spread inside before the potato filling is added, so the flavour comes through in every bite. An extra cup of ghee is provided with each dosa, which is nice - they make the ghee-flooding a consensual act - very woke of them :) You can simply return the cup of ghee if you don’t want to flood your dosa with it.

The Masala Dosa at Taaza Thindi in Jayanagar (called Arogya Ahaarain HSR, a sister concern, so exact same quality) proves that great food does not need a huge price tag. It is crisp, simple, and priced like it is still 2002. It quietly humiliates places charging four times (you know who I mean). I’m also a fan of their idlis, crisp vadas and their upma (upitu).

No honourable-mentions list would be complete without the Benne Masala Dosa at CTR, also known as Shri Sagar, in Malleswaram. The restaurant is more than a century old, and its dosa is roasted with a slab of white butter thick enough to spot from across the room. It is served on the same steel plates it always has been, to a queue that never seems to shrink, no matter how early you arrive.

These three are not on the numbered list because ranking them would feel almost disrespectful. They belong in a category of their own.

If you go and actually eat every dosa on this list, then tweet me at @kjb_ak on X, and you will unlock a rare, hidden secret dosa in your DMs. Good luck to you.

entry.title: Ooty Weekender
entry.content:
Long weekend janmashtami trip to Ooty.

From bangalore, we took the vande bharat to Coimbatore, then auto to the Coimbatore New Bus Stand or locally often called the Ooty bus stand. At the bus stand there was already a bus just about to depart to ooty that was almost full, instead of rushing for it, we saw another one in the bus bay waitiing that was mostly empty and got into that. 10 minutes later, we had started and paid Rs 75 per person for it to Ooty.

The bus stops at a few key places between coimbatore and ooty including Mettupalayam and Coonoor/Wellington. It took about 1.5 hours to mettupalayam and stopped halfway between that and coonoor for about 10-15minutes for a bathroom/tea break.

I wonder what it takes to become the rest stop choice for government buses. It's constant business with customers stuck with no choice to go anywhere else in the middle of the highway and a 5 minute window or risk missing the bus.

Another 2 hours from there to Ooty bus stand. We had started the trip at 11:40 and reached at around 3pm, not too bad at all.

This trip was a chance to touch grass, literally and otherwise. Just stay away from computers and social media, read on the lawns, feel the sunlight and clean air and just laze on the hills of Karnataka garden.

Noteworthy food stops:

  • Cafe Sansara - near Karnataka Garden and has a direct view of the lake. Lovely breakfast, enjoyed the avocado toast and pretty decent coffee.
  • Birdhouse Cafe - in Coonoor, cute cafe with a connected shop that has all kinds of whimsical animal and nature themed decor and tchotchkes. We bought a pair of carved wooden geese with blue sweaters painted on them for home.
  • Moddy's - iconic shop, extremely touristed but at this off-season visit, was still worth a visit. Purchased a bunch of random treats to take home for friends and family. Hot choc was nice of course, but I'm beginning to learn that i might not be a thick hot chocolate enjoyer, i prefer the kind that's more of a hot chocolate-flavoured milk as a comfort drink.

Instead of risking a long journey by bus, we returned by cab (cost about 3.5k for a sedan from ooty to CBE along with a few unhurried stops on the way. Our driver was a fun, comical character, constantly joking around, pointing us to things we should know about the area and telling us stories from previous clientele and other jobs he has done in the past. The 3 hours flew by in no time and we made it back to bangalore in no time.

entry.title: China is building a lunar navigation and communications network. Lasers shine again in latest demonstration.
entry.content:
China announced last month that it has demonstrated two-way optical laser communications between Earth and its DRO-A satellite, which was launched in 2024 and put in a stable Distant Retrograde Orbit (DRO). Earlier this year during NASA’s Artemis II mission, the Orion spacecraft demonstrated the same high-data-rate communications technology at 2.5 times DRO-A’s downlink speed of 100Mbps. The technology could be used by each country to get high quality streams of astronaut landings on the Moon of China and the USA respectively later this decade and early next. Jack Congram has reported additional context on China’s optical communications advancements with satellites in Earth orbit.

Optical communication is one part of the stack of technologies required in building a comprehensive lunar navigation and communications (navcom) network. Last year, China cemented and further advanced its multi-component lead in building and demonstrating parts of such a network, which included autonomous navigation at the Moon, and achieving the first ever daytime Earth-Moon laser distance measurements with a lunar orbiter. This article explains the rationale for building a lunar navcom network, and summarizes and contextualizes each major component China has demonstrated towards the same.

Queqiao, China’s ambition to build a lunar navcom constellation

Under the collective label Queqiao, Chinese technologists have been conducting studies for a phased constellation of over a dozen satellites around the Moon. [In Chinese mythology, Queqiao is a bridge formed for the reunion of lovers after a long separation.] Such a satellite constellation would provide high-precision navigation as well as high-bandwidth communications services to lunar missions, as a “bridge” between Earth and the Moon which touts high area coverage & redundancy. Earlier studies focused on a navcom constellation that optimizes coverage availability for the lunar south pole, where most of the upcoming major robotic and crewed missions are expected to take place. The primary intent of Queqiao is to support China’s ambitious crewed lunar surface missions and then a full-fledged Moonbase called the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). Related work also involves China developing capabilities to monitor and track spacecraft across cislunar space, which is the region of space enveloping Earth and the Moon. The US intends to have similar capabilities, starting with the launch of Advanced Space’s Oracle spacecraft later this decade as a cislunar traffic monitor.

Since 2018, China has deployed two communications relay orbiters around the Moon, called Queqiao 1 and Queqiao 2. They relayed communications for the Chang’e 4 and Chang’e 6 missions respectively on the Moon’s farside. The US is yet to demonstrate this capability. Queqiao 2 will also relay communications for China’s upcoming Chang’e 7 and Chang’e 8 lunar landers, which CMSA (and not CNSA anymore) is now targeting to launch in 2027 and 2028 respectively. Also, the Queqiao 2 launch carried two experimental Tiandu CubeSats, which entered lunar orbit too to perform laser-based distance ranging and more, as elaborated in later in this article. In all, the Queqiao 2 mission has been testing and verifying technologies which will feed into China’s upcoming full-fledged navcom constellation.

In a paper published in the Chinese Journal of Space Science, researchers proposed that China should integrate their Queqiao lunar satellites with the existing Earthbound Tianlian ones, which notably serve China’s Tiangong space station, among other things. As Andrew Jones had highlighted, the proposal’s driving rationale is to substantially improve surface coverage time and area for China’s upcoming ambitious crewed lunar missions and then for the ILRS Moonbase. It would also allow redundancy if and when China faces ground station availability issues from its terrestrial partners across the globe.

Why build a navcom constellation around the Moon?

For one, such a system can enable cost-effective Moon missions since several spacecraft would no longer necessarily need to carry hefty communications hardware and rent as much ground infrastructure. Partner nations with smaller space budgets can take advantage of such a network to send their own lunar missions at lower costs, including to the less explored farside. A navcom constellation can especially aid crew and hardware on the Moon’s poles by relaying communications, where direct Earth visibility is limited due to our planet being way lower on the horizon than for near-equatorial sites. A navcom constellation will also aid future rovers hunting for lunar water by allowing them to stay connected as they venture inside permanently shadowed regions, where direct Earth visibility worsens further. Moreover, lunar navcom satellites can provide a common time reference for the Moon, which would help swarms of lunar spacecraft operate safely. It would also improve the accuracy of lunar-based fundamental physics and astronomy experiments, including farside radio astronomy measurements.

Time synchronization between lunar satellites has become increasingly important to coordinate orbits in order to operate safely. But a common lunar time of some sort will also enable synergistic operations. To both ends, last year Chinese researchers released a first-of-its-kind software package to enable engineers to coordinate Moon and Earth times for multiple lunar missions in an integrated fashion. The authors consider the timing accuracy of this initial work to be sufficient for coordinating spacecraft over the next decade, and note that improvements will follow. What’s commendable is that the software is public on GitHub, and the paper describing the work and methodology open access. The project is being funded by the Chinese government institutions of CAS and NSFC.

Who else is planing lunar navcom constellations?

Other than China, ESA also aims to have a lunar navcom constellation with its Moonlight initiative. The UK’s SSTL-built, 280-kilogram Lunar Pathfinder orbiter will constitute ESA’s first Moonlight satellite out of five. It’s planned for launch onboard Firefly’s second Moon mission part of NASA’s CLPS program later this year or early next. ESA will be Moonlight’s anchor customer but expects European companies to actively commercially provide lunar navcom services to missions globally. On the US side, NASA is planning a navcom constellation called the Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS). The first satellite in this network, Intuitive Machines’ Altus-1, will launch onboard the company’s third CLPS lander next year. Furthermore, ispace Japan and US-based Argo Corp had announced this year that the duo aim to deploy at least five lunar navcom satellites by 2030, with the first one aimed for 2027.

Against the odds, China achieved an Earth-Moon navigation link

China managed to put the aforementioned DRO-A spacecraft and its twin DRO-B into their intended lunar distant retrograde orbits (DRO) in 2024 despite a failure of the upper stage of their launch vehicle Long March 2C. Qiu Chenhui of China Youth Daily reported based on a presentation in April last year by a Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) researcher Zhang Hao on how their team managed to achieve the feat.

The upper stage deployed the attached DRO-A-B craft with a high spin rate of once every 1.8 seconds, which bent and damaged their solar panels. While the satellite operators quickly stabilized the craft and figured out dynamic optimal solar panel orientations to stay power positive, the anomalous launch had also left the small satellites at less than half the distance from the Moon than intended. Within days, the team took a key decision to not separate the twin spacecraft and alternately use either craft’s engines to perform precisely timed orbit-raising maneuvers which conserve and balance fuel availability. It worked. Combined with this fuel-efficient, low energy trajectory to the Moon generated as contingency, the still attached DRO-A-B craft entered lunar orbit and DRO in August 2024. The two craft separated from each other shortly after. It was only days later that DRO-A and DRO-B fulfilled their primary mission objective: establish a laser-based navigation, timing, and communications link between themselves and the Earth-orbiting DRO-L satellite. Since then, the three craft have been able to track each other and navigate autonomously instead of relying heavily on, or choking, terrestrial ground stations.

This was a notable world first. And with it, not only did China avoid a mission failure but it cemented its lead in building a lunar communications and navigation network. The NASA-funded and Advanced Space-led CAPSTONE lunar orbiter has made some progress in cross-communicating with NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) since over three years now to perform similar Moon-to-Moon demonstrations but with a relatively limited scope and success than the Sino-DRO trio.

As an unrelated but interesting tangent, DRO-A also touts all-sky detection of gamma-ray bursts from highly energetic cosmic objects. This is achieved through placing of five detectors across four sides of the craft. The same has thus been enabling extended mission objectives, and continued the trend of China maximizing spacecraft capacity and time.

Tangent: Repurposing lunar missions to enable deep space exploration

Maneuvering with fluidity, lasers on target

Last year, China successfully made daytime Earth-Moon distance measurements wherein a 1.2-meter telescope reflected an infrared laser off of a small retroreflector on the 61-kilogram Tiandu-1 lunar orbiter. This was the first ever daytime laser distance measurement using an orbiter, accomplished despite massive interference from our Sun. Tiandu-1 was launched alongside Queqiao 2 in March 2024. The CASC release about the daytime distance measurements stated that the demonstration will “support the argumentation and implementation of major deep-space exploration projects in the future, such as the International Lunar Research Station” [Moonbase].

Ling Xin had reported that last year in May, China moved Tiandu 1 from DRO to a 3:1 resonance orbit, where it loops around Earth thrice for every revolution of the Moon around our planet. It’s a stable orbit, requiring minimal maintenance. It reminds me of how in 2023, ISRO pulled Chandrayaan 3’s propulsion module from lunar orbit to Earth orbit, demonstrating a small but key capability that will be required to pull off a robotic sample return mission in the future with Chandrayaan 4. Coming back to China, another spacecraft was maneuvered out of DRO last year. As per graphics published by CAS and subsequently reported by others, CAS made the DRO-B lunar satellite depart DRO in April and enter a 3:2 resonance orbit—a world first.

The damaged solar panels of DRO-B post its anomalous launch do reduce the extent of automated navigation the craft can perform in its new orbit with the other DRO satellites but demonstrations and spacecraft operations continued nevertheless. Enthusiastic spacecraft observer Scott Tilley, who has tracked Chinese lunar satellites and independently confirmed many of their orbits, has pointed out that Chinese researchers have published a paper on exactly these kinds of orbital maneuvers. From paper to practice, China has now demonstrated several low-energy orbital transfers as well as autonomous navigation in complex multi-body gravitational environments.

Queqiao 2 and looking beyond the Moon

China is doing more still in the Earth-Moon space. With the immediate mission of Queqiao 2 of enabling the Chang’e 6 spacecraft modules to fetch farside lunar samples being accomplished in 2024, the orbiter then began making observations to pursue its other scientific goals. This includes using it for the Astrophysics technique of Very Long Baseline interferometry (VLBI), which helps determine observer orientations with respect to celestial objects. CASC provided an update on Queqiao 2 last year in May:

The satellite has been stably operating in orbit for 14 months. [...] The satellite’s extreme ultraviolet camera captured the first global 83.4-nanometer ionosphere image, providing crucial data for studying the impact of solar activity on the plasmasphere. The satellite’s VLBI experiment system, in coordination with the Shanghai 65m Radio Telescope, extended the observation baseline to 380,000 kilometers and successfully observed deep-space targets like radio source A00235 and the Chang’e-6 orbiter.

At the time, Chinese researchers were expected to publish results based on these observations within a year. Checking in on the same, that has manifested. Chinese researchers have also suggested that when coupled with Earth-based ground stations, China’s lunar navcom network can help the country track its deep space missions with sub-kilometer accuracy all the way to Jupiter, and even beyond. As noted by Chi Wang, et al. in a December 2023 paper, Queqiao 2 will try testing an element of this during the upcoming Chang’e 7 Moon mission:

The LOVEX [payload] on the relay satellite is used [sic] to construct a 400,000-km baseline Moon–Earth VLBI measurement and observation experiment system to improve the accuracy of orbit determination in deep space and to carry out astrometry and astrophysics observation and study.

How China has an edge in sustaining future crewed Moon missions over the US

When considering all the developments above, it becomes clear that China has an extended, multi-component lead over the US in lunar navigation, communications, and related complex orbital operations. Other than Orion’s laser communications demonstration, the US did demonstrate a GPS lock on the Moon through private company Firefly’s first CLPS Moon lander last year but that’s pretty much it. The NASA-funded and Advanced Space-led CAPSTONE lunar orbiter’s autonomous navigation goals will have to be demonstrated firmly by the upcoming CAPSTONE 02 instead. ESA is yet to launch its first Moonlight satellite, and so is NASA its first navcom mission.

In contrast, China’s visibly great progress in building a full-fledged Queqiao lunar navcom constellation is bound to substantially improve both the surface coverage time and area for China’s upcoming ambitious crewed lunar missions, which along with robotic explorers will systematically lead up to the ILRS Moonbase. ILRS is a long-term undertaking, and the Queqiao constellation’s capabilities will afford China redundancy even if—or when—there are ground station availability issues from its terrestrial partners across the globe.

This year NASA rejigged the Artemis program elements & crewed missions, and has been catalyzing its Moonbase plans, in an effort to gain momentum after over a decade of lapses. While Artemis III is now supposed to be a test mission in Earth orbit ahead of attempting to land humans on the Moon with Artemis IV, the former won’t “test like you fly” since challenges confront NASA across aspects of both missions, including Starship’s repeated lapses and Blue Origin’s explosive delay chain. Even if the US somehow lands humans on the Moon first with Artemis IV later this decade, the long term game of sustaining human and robotic lunar presence currently favors China because it has demonstrated and achieved more complex capabilities in orbital infrastructure as well as modern surface missions, gaining valuable operational experiences therein.

Head Empty

I have been dealing with my anxiety by trying to reframe my mind. If you are dealing with something similar I hope what I write here can help a little bit.

  • The first is that I am trying more actively to counter the negative thought loop which springs up from time to time when I recieve neutral or ambiguous inputs. So now when I catch myelf thinking something like what if this person doesn't like me or what if this situation blows up in my face? I try to counter them by actively thinking that what if something good happens? what if these people don't actually hate you! Everyone wants you to succeed. That positive thought loop helps me calm down.

  • Another thing which I read recently was "You are a finite number of rejections away from getting what you want." It is a form of rejection therapy which I would like to share with you. In case you are afraid of getting rejected because it does really cause psychic type damage, you can and must try to take it in an excited way, because it means that you are one fewer "no" away from getting what you need. There was a prompt this week in the indie web meet about writing about a powerful experience I have had lately, and I think these two pattern breaking thought loops are something I would like to share. I hope it helps.

I am also working on self actualization, but I don't have much to share on that front yet. I'll keep you updated.

Oh No, My Software, It's Broken

This week felt like it went by pretty quickly.

#Life

I have been giving a few interviews lately, mostly just to keep myself up to date with what people are expecting these days from roles and AI. For a change, writing without any AI assistance during the interview felt nice. I had to roughly implement a Coordinator module for Reinforcement Learning, which was the first time I’d written anything about it. Didn’t go that well, but welp!

I also got my Schengen Visa approved :) Although, I had to call Bluedart customer support because the guy just mentioned “delivery address incorrect/incomplete” and didn’t even call me? Thankfully, it got delivered later that same day 🎉 🎉

On top of that, I also got promoted at $WORK to the next level! I’m grateful for it, but not entirely sure how to feel about it yet.

#The Odyssey

I know, I know. I watched this very late, but I didn’t want to pay ₹2000 per ticket for a movie (fake IMAX btw) in India. So Harsh, Swapnil, and I went on Tuesday morning at 7:45 AM because why not? (Well, the tickets were cheap, like ₹250/person.)

The movie was great, as I’d expect from a Nolan movie, and I enjoyed it overall. I think I also prefer this morning timing since you can get done with all of it by mid-day!

We then went to the newly opened LEGO Store just for some window shopping, and later, for breakfast, we decided to go try out Shyam Ji’s Chole Bhature. They were delicious, and I’m getting hungry just writing about it…

There was another small tea shop right beside it where we sat and talked for another 30 minutes while enjoying the morning. Honestly, a great start to the day ☀️

I should do this more often!

#Homelab

I was refactoring my dotfiles this week to use proper alphabetical numbering for all my ports [commit], and it broke a lot of things in places I didn’t even realize were using them 😭

In particular, it broke my main home proxy because I had a specific port allowed in the firewall rule that I had to change. I also had to fix Caddy’s load-balancing checks because it used to always try the first URL and take 5-10s to load [fix].

A few other things also decided to stop working:

  • Smart Search broke on Immich because the ML port changed [commit]
  • My *arr stack connections broke because of a non-code dependency :/
  • qBittorrent WebUI also broke since I use qui and have to manually add the port
  • Jellyfin broke because I hadn’t set its port in code either [commit]

One thing I still haven’t fixed is the Postgres port since everything broke :P and I was too lazy to change that for now.

There were also some other minor issues that had been around for quite some time, and the clanker allowed me to fix those pretty easily :)

  • When I cleared the cache on my server, my SSO (Authelia) sessions used to disappear, which was a pain because everyone had to log in again and again. Turns out this was due to a missing Redis host in the session config [commit]
  • Similar to the above issue, I had a misconfigured path for my Linkding instance, which also used to remove favicons etc. [commit]
  • Gatus logo was also broken because I removed it while rebuilding my website [commit]

I also moved my Frigate service from HAOS to my NixOS server and also added Vaultwarden to my stack. Moving 2FAs from other apps was a pain though 🫠

I’m not touching this for months now.
